Results: History- A previously healthy 15 year-old-teenager presented with a 3 year
history of moderate joint pain and stiffness of his back and extremities. More recent-
ly, there was a rapid progression of his symptoms, leading to a 6 week absence from
school and extracurricular activities. There was no response to NSAIDs or steroid
therapy.
Examination- Musculoskeletal examination revealed multiple contractures of large
and small joints with no evidence of arthritis. All joints had decreased passive and
active range of movement limited by pain and lead-pipe rigidity. Diffuse soft tissue
tenderness was elucidated. There was no evidence of enthesitis or tendonitis. Muscle
spasms were precipitated by tactile stimulation. A mild intention tremor was present.
He had a fixed hyperlordosis.
Investigations- Blood work was normal including autoantibody testing. All imaging
studies and nerve conduction testing were unremarkable. EMG demonstrated contin-
uous muscle activity at rest and during muscle relaxation. There was simultancous
activity of agonist and antagonist muscles.
Diagnosis: Stiff-person syndrome.
Treatment: IV-Immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment of 2g/kg monthly for 2months and
oral carbamazepine provided a significant reduction in the severity of joint pain and
stiffness at the three month review. There was a significant reduction in the number of
falling episodes and a return to full-time school.
Conclusion: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by progressive
axial rigidity with super-imposed muscle spasms leading to difficulty ambulating. It
has been postulated that the disorder is autoimmune with 65% positivity for anti-GAD
antibodies. The proposed diagnostic criteria include clinical features of fixed hyper-
lordosis, superimposed episodic muscle spasms and a normal neurological examina-
tion with EMG findings of continuous motor unit activity at rest. This patient had clin-
ical and investigative features to support the diagnosis of Stiff-person syndrome and a
good therapeutic response to IVIG. This case highlights the need to consider less com-
mon diagnoses for debilitating joint complaints in pediatric patients.
